stories.title: Japan's MMX mission is about to launch to bring back a piece of Phobos
paragraphs: The Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) is targeting launch of its Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft from Tanegashima Space Center at 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19 (4:41 a.m. JST on Tuesday, Oct. 20; that's 12:41 p.m. PT on Oct. 19), according to NASA. The mission aims to work out the origin of Mars's moons Phobos and Deimos and bring a sample of Phobos back to Earth.

MMX is scheduled to reach Mars in August 2027, NASA says. New Scientist reports that it will enter an orbit that keeps it alongside Phobos to map the surface, observing Deimos along the way, and use the map to pick a landing site. During one or two brief landings, it is to drop off a small rover called IDEFIX, the first rover placed on such a small body, and collect samples. NASA says sampling will happen no earlier than December 2028, with delivery to Earth in 2031.

NASA is contributing the MEGANE spectrograph, which measures gamma rays and neutrons to determine what Phobos is made of, and the Pneumatic Sampler (P-Sampler), which collects surface material with bursts of high-pressure nitrogen. JAXA's C-Sampler will take cores from a few inches deeper. Honeybee Robotics, a Blue Origin company, developed the pneumatic sampler mechanism. NASA's Deep Space Network will provide communications and navigation support, and ESA says it is contributing deep-space communication technology and ground station support. NASA will receive and curate about 15% of the returned sample at Johnson Space Center.

The samples are meant to settle a long debate over where the two moons came from. "Phobos and Deimos may be the remains of a massive impact on Mars that sent material into orbit around the planet, or they could be ancient asteroids that were captured by Mars' gravity billions of years ago," said Tom Statler, MMX program executive and program scientist at NASA. "Having the answer will help illuminate that early era when Earth and the other inner planets may have been acquiring much of their water and organic compounds." New Scientist notes that the moons' shapes resemble asteroids, while their circular orbits over Mars's equator fit the impact idea better.

stories.title: Artemis II's first science results: tiny meteorite impacts and the moon's hidden colors
paragraphs: Six months after NASA's Artemis II crew flew around the moon in April, the mission's science team released its first results on October 7: three reports and a large data archive, three days ahead of the team's six-month deadline after the April 10 splashdown. Science News reported on the findings, which were presented at a virtual Lunar Surface Science Workshop meeting.

During a 54-minute stretch when the moon eclipsed the sun, the crew spotted five impact flashes, which Jennifer Heldmann of NASA Ames described as "pinpricks of light lasting less than a second." By comparing the flash rate with impact models, the team estimated the rocks weighed about 8.5 grams and were just over 4.5 centimeters across, roughly golf-ball size. Heldmann said the crew likely set a record for the smallest meteorites ever optically observed hitting the moon. She put the chance of a dangerous impact during a two-week surface mission like the planned Artemis IV at less than 1 in 10 million.

The crew's spoken and written descriptions turned out to be among the most valuable data, according to the science team. Combined with data going back to the 1970s, their color observations were linked to composition: blues with titanium-rich volcanic rock, browns with differing iron levels and greens with glass from eruptions or impacts.

The team also listed lessons for future missions. The astronauts' cameras weren't calibrated before flight because of time constraints, and the pairing of two crew members at the windows with two talking to the ground led to better science, the team concluded. NASA separately published underwater imagery of the Orion heat shield taken by U.S. Navy divers shortly after splashdown.

stories.title: Leap seconds will be abolished in favor of a 'leap hour'
paragraphs: Representatives from 69 countries voted on 15 October, at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Versailles, France, to stop adding leap seconds to coordinated universal time (UTC), New Scientist reports. Instead, UTC will be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time before being corrected. The change takes effect from 20 May 2027.

Leap seconds have kept atomic-clock time in step with Earth's slightly irregular rotation since 1972, and 27 have been added. New Scientist reports that modern systems from stock markets to telecoms and GPS depend on precise time, making leap seconds risky. Setnam Shemar of the UK's National Physical Laboratory said past leap seconds have crashed websites and disrupted airline booking systems.

Earth's rotation has recently begun to speed up slightly, raising the possibility of "a first-ever negative leap second", said Noël Dimarcq, head of the BIPM's committee on time and frequency. He said the leap hour should give an uninterrupted flow of time for "several centuries". Shemar said it will be "many hundreds or even thousands of years before a leap hour is needed."

The meeting also asked for proposals for a new definition of the second, because optical clocks are now more accurate than the caesium clocks it is based on, and called on international agencies to start work on a universal time standard for the moon.

stories.title: Meta releases Muse Spark Open, an 816-billion-parameter open-weight model
paragraphs: Meta announced Muse Spark Open on October 15 and calls it the "most capable US open-weight model to date," The Verge reports. According to The Decoder, it has 816 billion total parameters (42 billion active), up to one million tokens of context, and handles text, image, video and audio. Meta says it is built for coding and agentic tasks.

On Meta's own benchmark results, reported by The Decoder, the model leads open models such as Qwen 3.8, GLM 5.3 and Kimi K3 in several agentic, knowledge and multimodal categories but trails some competitors on coding benchmarks and falls well short of Meta's paid Muse Wonder Full models.

Meta and Apple worked together on the launch. Meta says the model can run locally on two Apple M5 Ultra Mac Studios using Apple's MLX framework, and The Decoder reports that each Mac Studio has 512 GB of unified memory. Mark Zuckerberg and Apple CEO John Ternus both praised the collaboration on X, according to The Verge.

The weights are on Hugging Face. The Decoder reports the license is free to use but requires a "Built with Muse Spark Open" label, and providers with more than $20 million in annual revenue who want to offer it as an API service need a separate agreement with Meta.

stories.title: Google's Gemini 4 Argon passes 95% on ARC-AGI-3, with caveats
paragraphs: Google DeepMind's new frontier model, Gemini 4 Argon, scored 97.5 percent on the ARC-AGI-3 benchmark at a cost of $4,800, The Decoder reports, citing ARC Prize. That makes Google the second lab after OpenAI to pass 95 percent on the test. Only OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra scores higher, at 99.9 percent.

The result depends heavily on the test setup. The 97.5 percent score used the "Provider Adapter Harness," which allows vendor-specific features such as retained reasoning and context compaction. In the "Standard Harness," Argon scored 49.8 percent at low reasoning. The testers said API problems kept it from finishing all 55 games, and no score was published for its highest reasoning setting.

Epoch AI rated Argon 165 on its Epoch Capabilities Index, which combines more than 50 benchmarks. That ties it with Fable 5.1, just behind Opus 5.5 (167) and GPT-6 Astra (166), and puts Google closer to the top than at any point since Gemini 3.1 Pro in February. Early Epoch estimates place it eighth in math and sixth in software engineering.
